title: Cryptography Foundations
summary: The vocabulary and guarantees of cryptography, what it actually promises versus what marketing claims, and the one ground rule — security lives in the key, not the algorithm's secrecy — that governs every topic in this group.

slides.markdown:
Cryptography is the one security topic where the guarantees are mathematically precise — which also means it's the one where sloppy language gets called out fastest. "Unbreakable," "military-grade," "quantum-proof" are marketing phrases, not cryptographic properties.

This topic sets up the vocabulary — plaintext, ciphertext, key, algorithm — and the two ideas that every other topic in this group depends on: cryptographic security is a **quantitative, not absolute** claim (measured in the computational cost to break it), and it must rest entirely on **key secrecy**, never on the algorithm being unknown.

Get these two ideas solid here, and hashing, symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption, and signatures all become variations on a theme rather than separate things to memorize.

slides.subTitle: "Unbreakable" is not a property
slides.markdown:
No cryptographic system is unbreakable in an absolute sense — given enough computational power and enough time, any encryption can be brute-forced by trying every possible key. What cryptography actually promises is narrower and more useful: **breaking it costs more computation than is remotely feasible, for as long as the data needs to stay protected.**

That's a quantitative claim, not a binary one. AES-256 isn't "unbreakable" — it's designed so that brute-forcing it would take longer than the age of the universe with any computing power currently conceivable, which is functionally the same thing for any practical purpose, but is a fundamentally different kind of claim than "cannot be broken."

This distinction matters because it explains why cryptographic recommendations change over time without any flaw being found: as computing power grows, what counted as "infeasible to brute-force" a decade ago (DES's 56-bit key) can become feasible today. The algorithm didn't get weaker — the cost of attacking it just changed relative to available compute.

Four terms used precisely throughout this entire group:

- **Plaintext** — the original, readable data before any transformation.
- **Ciphertext** — the scrambled output after encryption; unreadable without the right key.
- **Key** — the secret input that controls the transformation. Same algorithm, different key, completely different ciphertext.
- **Algorithm (cipher)** — the specific mathematical procedure that transforms plaintext to ciphertext and back, given a key. AES and RSA are algorithms; a specific AES key you generated for one application is a key.

The relationship that makes all of this work: **encrypt(plaintext, key) = ciphertext**, and **decrypt(ciphertext, key) = plaintext**, where the algorithm is public and reused across billions of different keys and messages. Confusing "algorithm" with "key" is the single most common vocabulary slip in this area — an algorithm is shared infrastructure; a key is what actually needs protecting.

![The encrypt/decrypt pipeline: plaintext to ciphertext and back, with the same key icon feeding both the encrypt and decrypt steps](assets/encryption-pipeline.svg)

Every cryptographic scheme in this group is a variation on this one shape. Symmetric encryption uses the *same* key for both arrows. Asymmetric encryption uses a *different but mathematically related* key for each arrow — encrypt with one, decrypt with the other. Hashing removes the decrypt arrow entirely, by design (more on why in the next topic). Keeping this one diagram in mind is what makes the more complex schemes ahead easy to place — each one changes exactly one thing about this picture.

slides.sectionTitle: Symmetric vs asymmetric, at a glance
slides.markdown:
| | Symmetric | Asymmetric |
|---|---|---|
| **Keys** | One shared key, used for both encrypt and decrypt | A key *pair* — public key encrypts, private key decrypts (or vice versa for signing) |
| **Speed** | Fast — designed for bulk data | Much slower — expensive math (factoring, elliptic curves) |
| **Key distribution problem** | Both parties need the *same* secret key beforehand — how do you share it safely? | The public key can be shared openly; only the private key must stay secret |
| **Typical use** | Encrypting the actual bulk data (files, traffic) | Exchanging a symmetric key, or signing |
| **Examples** | AES, ChaCha20 | RSA, ECC |

The key-distribution row is the whole reason both exist side by side rather than one replacing the other: symmetric is fast but needs a pre-shared secret, which is exactly the problem asymmetric crypto solves. Real systems — TLS, PGP — use asymmetric crypto to exchange a symmetric key, then switch to symmetric for the actual data, getting the best of both. This hybrid pattern is covered in full in Asymmetric (Public-Key) Cryptography.

slides.subTitle: Why AES-128 is "enough"
slides.markdown:
A brute-force attack tries every possible key until one works. Key length in bits determines how many keys exist: a 128-bit key has 2¹²⁸ possibilities — roughly 3.4 × 10³⁸.

To see why that number makes brute force hopeless, not just hard: even a hypothetical machine trying **a trillion keys per second** (far beyond any real hardware) would need on the order of 10¹⁸ years to exhaust half the key space on average — many times the current age of the universe. This is why AES-128 is considered fully secure against brute force today and will remain so for the foreseeable future; AES-256 exists mainly as margin against future cryptanalytic advances and, longer-term, quantum computers, not because AES-128's key space is remotely reachable.

This is also why key length comparisons across algorithm *families* are misleading without context — a 128-bit AES key and a 128-bit RSA key are not equivalently strong, because RSA's security rests on factoring difficulty, not brute-forcing a key space, and factoring is attackable by fundamentally different (and much faster) methods at a given bit length. Comparing "bits" only makes sense within the same algorithm family.

slides.subTitle: Security lives in the key
slides.markdown:
[Security Design Principles](security-design-principles) introduced Kerckhoffs's principle in general; cryptography is where it's non-negotiable. **AES and RSA are fully public specifications** — anyone can read the exact math, implement it from scratch, and run it. Their security depends entirely on the secrecy of the specific key used, never on the algorithm being unknown.

This is deliberate, and it's *why* these algorithms are trustworthy rather than despite it: a public algorithm gets attacked by every credible cryptanalyst on the planet for decades, and AES in particular has survived that scrutiny since 2001 with no practical break found. A private, unreviewed algorithm has faced approximately zero equivalent scrutiny — it hasn't been proven weak, but it also hasn't been proven anything, which is a very different state from "trusted."

The practical rule this produces: rotate and protect keys aggressively (short lifetimes, hardware security modules, strict access control) — that's your actual secrecy budget — and never treat the algorithm itself as something that needs to be hidden to work.

A recurring mistake, usually well-intentioned: a team decides a standard algorithm is "overkill" or wants something "more unique" and builds a custom encryption or obfuscation scheme — often little more than XOR with a repeating key, a home-rolled substitution cipher, or a proprietary "secret sauce" transformation.

This fails for a specific, structural reason, not just "it's risky": designing a cryptographic algorithm that resists decades of attack techniques — differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis, related-key attacks — is a specialized research discipline. AES itself was the winner of a multi-year open competition among the world's best cryptographers, specifically because getting this right by intuition doesn't work, even for very smart engineers. Custom schemes are broken constantly, often within hours of being examined by anyone who actually knows the field, precisely because they skip that adversarial review entirely.

The fix is never "invent your own" — it's use a standard, publicly vetted primitive (AES, RSA, ChaCha20) and put your engineering effort into using it correctly: proper modes of operation, unique nonces, secure key storage. Nearly every real-world crypto failure is a *misuse* of a good algorithm, not a flaw in the algorithm itself.

Vendor claims like "military-grade encryption" or "unbreakable, quantum-proof security" are a reliable signal to look more closely, not a reason for confidence — legitimate cryptography is described precisely ("AES-256-GCM"), not with marketing adjectives.

"Military-grade" usually just means AES, the same algorithm available in every modern programming language's standard library — it's accurate but meaningless as a differentiator, since AES *is* the commodity standard, not a special tier above it. "Unbreakable" contradicts the entire premise from earlier in this topic: security is a computational-cost claim, and any vendor asserting an absolute is either using loose language or doesn't understand what they're selling.

The useful questions to ask instead: which specific, named algorithm and mode is used (AES-256-GCM, not "AES" alone — mode matters, covered in Symmetric Encryption)? How are keys generated, stored, and rotated? Has the *implementation*, not just the algorithm choice, been independently audited? Precise, checkable answers are the actual signal of a system worth trusting.

Two ideas from this topic recur in every topic that follows: cryptographic strength is **measured in computational cost**, and it must rest **entirely on the key**, never the algorithm's secrecy.

From here, the group goes deeper on each side of the encrypt/decrypt pipeline: Hashing & Message Integrity covers the one-way variant that deliberately drops the decrypt step. Symmetric Encryption goes inside AES and the modes of operation that determine whether encryption actually holds up in practice. Asymmetric (Public-Key) Cryptography covers the key-pair side and why RSA and ECC are computationally expensive by design. Digital Signatures & PKI and Key Management close the group with how keys get trusted and managed at scale.

Every one of those topics is, underneath, a more detailed answer to a question this topic already set up: given the vocabulary and the two ground rules here, what specifically does each scheme guarantee, and what does it deliberately not guarantee?
